title: Build governed data apps with Microsoft Fabric Apps (Generally Available)
author: sapatney

content.text:
If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric.
AI has made it much faster to create an initial version of an app. Ask a coding agent to turn the spreadsheet your team uses to track supplier issues into an app, and it can be running in hours rather than days.
Putting that app in front of the business is another matter. It needs a database, sign-in, and access to company data that respects the permissions already in place, and IT needs to know the app exists. Left to wire this up alone, an agent takes the shortest path, which often means copying data where it shouldn’t go or sharing it with people who shouldn’t see it. Multiply that by every team with an agent and you get shadow IT at agent speed.
Rayfin and Microsoft Fabric apps address these deployment and governance challenges, and today at Microsoft Ignite, both are generally available. Developers and their agents build with Rayfin, our open-source SDK and CLI. When deployed, the app runs as a Fabric app, next to your data, behind Microsoft Entra sign-in, and under the governance you already have. We want every team to build like a startup and deploy like an enterprise.
Since preview, more than 100,000 apps have been created. Today’s release makes Rayfin and Fabric apps ready for production and adds PostgreSQL and file storage for developers, a single view of every app for administrators, and new ways to build from Microsoft Copilot and Power BI.
Figure: Animated GIF - Examples of data-rich business applications built with Microsoft Fabric apps. More examples can be found in the Fabric apps community gallery.
The whole app, defined in code
With Rayfin, the backend lives in the same project as the user interface. You describe your data and who can access it in TypeScript, and Rayfin generates the database and API with those rules enforced. One command, Rayfin up, deploys the whole app to Fabric.
We built it this way on purpose. It gives coding agents a consistent development model instead of requiring them to coordinate multiple cloud services independently. And because every app declares its data, permissions, and connections in one place, it’s easier to review and govern.
Figure: Rayfin defines app data, APIs, authentication, policies, functions, and hosting for local or Fabric deployment.
Every Fabric app can use:
• Databases: SQL database in Fabric, or the new Fabric HorizonDB (Preview), serverless PostgreSQL for teams and agents that default to Postgres.
• Authentication and permissions: Microsoft Entra sign-in and per-record access rules.
• Functions: server-side TypeScript for business logic, integrations, and calls to Microsoft Foundry models.
• Connectors: direct access to the semantic models, warehouses, lakehouses, and SQL databases you already have in Fabric.
• Storage: files, images, and documents, stored in OneLake.
• Observability: metrics, logs, and traces in Application Insights.
Because the app is defined in code, developers can use the same project across local and cloud environments. Rayfin Local runs the app and its back end on your laptop, even before you have a Fabric workspace. The Rayfin up command then publishes the same code to Fabric unchanged. The model is similar to developing in Power BI Desktop and publishing to the Power BI service: creators work locally and deploy to a managed service when they are ready to share.
That shared development model is already helping organizations reduce the handoffs between data experts and engineers. The Craneware Group, which helps healthcare providers optimize their financial performance, previously lost days or weeks as ideas moved between customers, data experts, engineering, and production. With Fabric apps, its data experts can build alongside engineers on a shared, governed foundation, helping ideas move from review to deployment without the wait.
“Fabric apps are changing the way we think about application development. Instead of treating data, analytics, AI, and the application as separate technology stacks, we can bring them together on a single governed platform and focus our engineering effort on creating value for customers.”
—Mark Sentell, VP of Product Development, The Craneware Group
Built on the data you already trust
Most organizations have spent years getting their data right, from certified semantic models to agreed definitions of revenue and margin. Fabric apps build on that work instead of starting over with another copy.
A Fabric app can query the same semantic models and measures as your Power BI reports, while retaining the security defined for that data. With the new Fabric IQ connector, people can also ask about that data in plain language. And decisions made in the app can be written back to governed tables in OneLake, ready for reporting and AI.
That foundation is already changing how teams put trusted data into action. At Thomson Reuters, the Monthly Business Review now runs as a Fabric app, built on the same certified Power BI semantic models that ground the company’s DeepVista AI framework and its agents in Microsoft Teams. By bringing trusted metrics, natural-language analysis, and review workflows into a single experience, the team spends less time reconciling numbers and more time deciding what to do next.
“This is a breakthrough in how Finance works. Certified semantic models give us numbers we can trust. Thomson Reuters DeepVista’s AI agents let analysts and leaders ask questions in natural language and get insights they can act on. The monthly business hub solution automates the business review, so we spend our time on what to do next.”
—Michael Goddard, Head of Corporate Finance, Thomson Reuters
Watch the interview with Thomson Reuters to see how they are innovating with Fabric.
Governed by default
As more people build with AI, apps will multiply faster than any IT team can review them one at a time. The controls have to live in the platform, not in a review queue.
Every Fabric app is a Fabric item, so it shows up in lineage, follows your workspace permissions and sharing rules, and runs on your capacity.
Capabilities for administrators with general availability:
• The Apps view in the OneLake governance hub: every app in the organization in one place, with the ability to block or unblock any of them.
• Content Security Policy (CSP): control over which external resources an app can load in the browser.
• Secure Embed: the option to require that apps run only inside an embedded frame.
• Item identity: apps reach data under their own identity, not the permissions of the person who deployed them.
Figure: Manage and govern Fabric apps across your organization with the Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub.
Build wherever you work
Professional developers will build in code with the agent they prefer. But many of the most useful apps will come from the people closest to the work, like the analyst who owns the forecast. They should be able to start in familiar Microsoft experiences and build on the same governed foundation.
• Microsoft Copilot: Turn a simple prompt into a working application, with the option to use Fabric as a managed backend for databases, storage, and data APIs through Copilot Managed Runtime. Apps can grow from simple ideas into data-rich business solutions without managing infrastructure.
• Power BI: We’re bringing Fabric apps to Power BI Pro, so many more Power BI users can build them. Power BI Desktop for apps turns an existing semantic model into an interactive app that runs on Fabric.
Get started
I expect that within a few years, building an app will be as ordinary as building a spreadsheet. When that happens, making an app enterprise-ready can’t be a separate project. With Rayfin and Fabric apps, it isn’t.
If you’re joining Ignite, in person or online, I’d start with these sessions:
• BRK355: Build like a startup. Deploy like an enterprise
• THR880: Rayfin: building the next generation of apps with enterprise data
• THR925: From prompt to production: Build a Fabric app live
• LAB690 (in person only): Ship AI apps fast with Rayfin, a managed backend as a service
To start building:
• Get the Rayfin SDK and CLI on GitHub.
• Explore the open-source tools and resources to start building applications locally with Rayfin. Explore the GitHub repository.
• Read the Fabric apps documentation.
• Browse the Fabric apps community gallery and share what you build.
